en: I meditate upon Gāyatrī, the beloved of Hari, who possesses three eyes and five faces; she who is the fruit of Viśvāmitra’s penance, most dear, frequented by hosts of Brahmins, bestowing the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal, with a smiling face radiant as the crescent moon, her countenance glowing with the red hue of betel, stationed in the midst of the sun, and adorned with the three-eyed Lord. 1.

I meditate upon Gāyatrī, who has three eyes and five faces, the beloved of Hari; she whose two feet are worshipped with jasmine, lotus, ketakī, and water-lily flowers; she who is endowed with a series of syllables whose essence is the meaning of reality and who bestows the wisdom of that same reality; she who is auspicious and is served by wise men devoted to the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).

I meditate upon Gāyatrī, the beloved of Hari, who possesses three eyes and five faces; she increases the beauty of all the worlds with the sounds of her anklets, dispels great hosts of Rākṣasas by the water stirred by Brahmins, removes the sins of the one who recites her, resembles the Japā flower, and is graced by a swan.

I meditate upon the three-eyed, five-faced Gāyatrī, adorned with a girdle of fine cloth, whose nature is Śiva; who bears a single garland, a half-garland, and other ornaments; the Supreme Goddess, the giver of refuge, who cuts through the intellect blinded by delusion; who is the triple city beginning with the earth, the mother of the three worlds, praised in the branches of the inner self (adhyātma), the beloved of Hari.

I meditate upon Gāyatrī, the beloved of Hari, who has three eyes and five faces; she removes the heat of the fire within the womb of the meditator, consists of the Sāman, is sung as the Sāma-veda, is well-served at the hour of twilight, is composed of the musical notes (svaras), and is dark-green like the blade of a dūrvā grass; she is graced by the lord of kheṭīs whose mind is solely intent on the service of her mother, and is adorned with a garland.

I meditate upon Gāyatrī, the beloved of Hari, who has three eyes and five faces; she is served by the most excellent Brahmins shining in garments variegated with the hues of twilight; she wears beautiful pearl garlands of stars; within her radiant jewel-moon jars are the finest gems; she possesses a face like the full moon of the Rākā night; she is praised by the Lord of Ramā; and her hands shine with the conch and other emblems.

I meditate upon Gāyatrī, the beloved of Hari, who has three eyes and five faces; she is eternally adorned by bees that hum with the sound of her braided hair, she possesses the humming of bees wandering through the palace of her tongue which knows the elixir of the essence of reality, and she dispels the evening darkness with the moonbeam-like rays of the pearl adorning her nose.

I meditate upon Gāyatrī, the beloved of Hari, who has three eyes and five faces; she whose forehead shines with the saffron dust from the space between the lotus-feet of Rāma, who is uniquely relishing the sight of Rambhā’s dance, who bestows the wisdom of Vedānta, and who listens to the sounds of lute, flute, drum, and cymbals produced by the gods. 8.

Having severed the mountain-like sins of killing, drinking intoxicants, stealing gold, and violating the bed of a guru—sins as formidable as Indra—the Brahmins, who are like the sun, recite the Gāyatrī with one-pointed minds during the twilights; having chanted this mantra of the Goddess, these Vaidikas attain the supreme goal. (9)
Thus ends the Gāyatrī-aṣṭaka composed by the illustrious Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrīmacchaṅkarācārya.
